sentences.text: Giganotosaurus is considered one of the largest theropod dinosaurs that lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Early Cretaceous.
The holotype specimen has been estimated to be between 12 and 13 meters long, standing over 4 meters high at the hips.
Its hind legs featured a femur longer than the tibia, indicating strong support rather than high speed.
The shoulder girdle of this animal was proportionally shorter compared to the similar Tyrannosaurus.
The premaxilla bone possessed four tooth sockets, a feature also seen in Acrocanthosaurus and Sinraptor.
The jaw articulated far behind the neck attachment point, and the curvature of the lower jaw suggests it had a wide mouth.
A large dentary bone suggests that some individuals may have reached a weight of 10 metric tons, making them potentially larger than Tyrannosaurus.
Researchers concluded that Giganotosaurus reached the maximum possible size for a strictly bipedal animal.
Giganotosaurus is one of the largest known theropods, estimated to reach lengths of 12 to 13 meters, a skull over 1.60 meters long, and a weight of 7 to 8 tons.
The genus Giganotosaurus was described by Coria and Salgado in 1995.
The holotype specimen was discovered in the Candeleros Formation of Patagonia in 1993 by the fossil hunter Rubén Darío Carolini.
The Candeleros Formation containing these fossils was composed of sandstones deposited in fluvial and aeolian environments.
Giganotosaurus is thought to have been homeothermic with a metabolism between that of a mammal and a reptile, enabling fast growth.
The animal was capable of closing its jaws quickly to capture and bring down prey with powerful bites.
In 1999 and 2002, paleontologist Reese E. Barrick and geologist William J. Showers found that Giganotosaurus had oxygen isotope patterns similar to Tyrannosaurus.
While absolute bite force values in newtons were impossible to estimate, Giganotosaurus had a weaker bite force than Tyrannosaurus.
Giganotosaurus had a strong neck with a robust axis vertebra, and the rear neck vertebrae had short, flattened bodies with almost hemispherical front articulations.
Giganotosaurus was likely the largest predator of its time, occupying the top of the food chain.
Fossil tracks attributed to Giganotosaurus range from 36 cm to 50 cm in length with paces between 100 cm and 130 cm.
The footprints of Giganotosaurus are three-toed with large, coarse digits and prominent impressions of claws.
Coria and Salgado originally classified Giganotosaurus as belonging to the Tetanurae clade rather than basal theropods like ceratosaurs.
According to a 2016 study by Apesteguía et al., Giganotosaurus belongs to the family Carcharodontosauridae.
Giganotosaurus lived between 99 and 95 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Patagonia, Argentina.

It is debated whether Giganotosaurus was larger than Tyrannosaurus, roughly equal in size, or if its largest size estimates are exaggerated. In 1997, Coria estimated Giganotosaurus to be 13.7 to 14.3 meters long and weigh 8 to 10 metric tons, larger than Carcharodontosaurus. A large dentary bone suggests that some Giganotosaurus individuals may have reached a weight of 10 metric tons, making them potentially larger than Tyrannosaurus.
Coria suggested that a bonebed of Giganotosaurus relatives was the result of a catastrophic event and that the mix of ages indicated these large theropods hunted in packs.
